sources.title: PrimeRange executable Java validation plus independent reviewer naive oracle
Prime range candidate independent source-first review

claims.text: The preserved source asks to print primes in 101~200 and report the count; inclusive interval interpretation, Java API and algorithm choice are answer-side decisions.
A composite integer has a factor at or below its square root, so checking the inclusive sqrt boundary is sufficient; after handling 2, only odd candidate divisors are needed.
Under the explicit inclusive [101,200] interpretation, an independent naive reviewer oracle and the Java fixture both produce the exact 21-number prime list stated in the candidate.
The executable implementation covers n<2, 2, even composites, square composites and a reusable int loop-overflow guard, and agrees with a naive divisor oracle on every integer -20..500.

validation.reported_stdout: PASS fixed-range=21 exact-list=yes oracle=-20..500 boundaries=yes square-composites=yes

findings: The preserved source is a singleton coding question asking to print all primes in 101~200 and report their count; it does not preserve a programming language, API shape, primality algorithm or an explicit open/closed interval convention.
The candidate makes the consequential interval choice explicit as an answer-side inclusive [101,200] interpretation instead of presenting it as recovered source wording.

The primality argument is correct: every composite n has at least one factor not exceeding sqrt(n), so after 2 is handled separately it is sufficient to test odd divisors through the inclusive square-root boundary.

The implementation uses d <= n/d, avoiding d*d overflow in the reusable int helper while preserving the intended square-root stopping condition; the displayed helper and executable helper are aligned after remediation.

Under the declared inclusive interpretation, an independent naive reviewer oracle yields exactly 21 primes: 101 through 199 with the same explicit list as the candidate; 121 and 169 confirm the inclusive square-root boundary.
The standalone Java implementation also matches a separate naive divisor oracle for every integer from -20 through 500 and preserves the fixed-range output/count contract.
The answer does not fabricate production experience or source constraints; sieve/segmented-sieve discussion is explicitly framed as an extension beyond the fixed interview problem.
